title: Europe and Comparing States, c. 1200–1450
subject: AP World History
objectives: Explain how feudalism and manorialism organized political and economic power in medieval Europe
Explain the role of the Roman Catholic Church and the division between Catholic and Orthodox Christianity
Explain how the Crusades, revival of trade, growth of towns, and the Black Death drove change in late medieval Europe
Compare state-building across regions from c. 1200 to c. 1450 and apply the historical reasoning skill of comparison

sections.heading: The Continent of a Thousand Rulers
sections.content:
Imagine you are a peasant in France around the year 1250. Who governs your life? Not really the king — you may never see him and he has limited power over your village. Your real ruler is the local lord whose manor you farm, who collects your dues, judges your disputes, and can call up knights for war. Above him are greater lords; above them, dukes; and somewhere at the top, a king who depends on all those lords to lend him soldiers and rarely commands them directly. Power in medieval Europe was not concentrated in a capital — it was scattered down a ladder of personal loyalties, like a pyramid built of handshakes.

That fragmentation is the single most important thing to understand about Europe in this period, and it produces a striking contrast with the societies you've already studied. While Song China ran a vast centralized bureaucracy chosen by examination, and Dar al-Islam shared a sophisticated common culture, western Europe was comparatively poor, rural, decentralized, and — by the standards of the day — something of a backwater. This is not an insult to Europe; it is a fact about 1250 that makes the later 'rise of the West' genuinely surprising and worth explaining.

This lesson has two jobs, so read it with both in mind. The first job is content: understand how medieval Europe was organized (feudalism and manorialism), what held it together culturally (the Catholic Church), and how it began to change (trade, towns, monarchies, and the catastrophe of the Black Death). The second job is a thinking skill: comparison. Unit 1 ends by asking you to compare states across the whole world around 1200–1450, and the comparison essay (LEQ) is a major exam task. So as we examine Europe, we'll constantly hold it up against China, the Islamic world, and the Americas — and then learn the formal method for writing a comparison.

Keep one question running in your head throughout: not just 'what was Europe like?' but 'how was Europe similar to and different from the other societies of this era, and why?' That second question is the AP World mindset.

sections.heading: Feudalism and Manorialism: A Decentralized World
sections.content:
Two interlocking systems organized medieval European life. The political-military system was feudalism: a web of personal agreements in which a lord granted land (a fief) to a vassal, and in return the vassal owed military service, loyalty, and counsel. A king granted land to great nobles, who granted portions to lesser knights, each bound to the man above him. The result was a chain of obligations rather than a centralized state — and because each lord commanded his own knights and castle, real power was distributed, not held at the top.

Underneath feudalism sat its economic engine: manorialism. A manor was a largely self-sufficient agricultural estate, the lord's land worked by peasants. Most of those peasants were serfs — not enslaved, but legally bound to the land, unable to leave without permission, owing labor and a share of their crops to the lord in exchange for protection and the right to farm. The manor produced most of what it needed and traded little; this was an economy of land and obligation, not of money and markets. Compare this with the bustling commercial economy of Song China, with its paper money and proto-industry, and you immediately feel how rural and localized Europe was.

Why was Europe so decentralized? Largely because there was no strong central state to provide order after the fall of the western Roman Empire centuries earlier. In a dangerous, fragmented world, people traded freedom for protection: a serf accepted bondage to a lord who could defend the manor, and a knight accepted obligations to a greater lord who could organize defense. Feudalism and manorialism were, in a sense, a society's improvised answer to the absence of a unifying government — a very different answer from the Chinese bureaucracy or the Inca command state, but an answer to the same universal problem of organizing power and security.

sections.heading: The Church: Europe's Unifying Thread — and Its Great Divide
sections.content:
If political power in Europe was fragmented, one institution reached across all the borders: the Roman Catholic Church. In a continent of competing lords and weak kings, the Church was the closest thing to a unifying authority. Nearly everyone in western Europe was Catholic; the Pope in Rome claimed spiritual authority over all of them; church law touched marriage, morality, and daily life; and the rhythm of the year was set by Christian festivals. The Church was also enormously wealthy and powerful in worldly terms — one of the largest landholders in Europe, collecting tithes and able to influence kings.

The Church did important cultural work, too. Monasteries preserved literacy and copied ancient texts through centuries when few others could read, keeping fragments of classical learning alive. Universities, which grew up under church influence from the 1100s, became centers of scholarship. In a decentralized world, the Church provided a shared identity, a shared language of scholarship (Latin), and a shared moral framework — playing a role somewhat like the one Confucianism played in East Asia or Islam in Dar al-Islam, a cultural glue that held a region together when politics did not.

But Christianity itself was not one unified faith. The great split — the Schism of 1054 — had already divided Christianity into the Roman Catholic Church in the west, led by the Pope, and the Eastern Orthodox Church in the east, centered on the Byzantine Empire and its capital Constantinople, where the emperor held great authority over the church. The Byzantine Empire was the surviving eastern half of the Roman Empire, far more centralized, urban, and wealthy than western Europe — and it spread Orthodox Christianity, along with its alphabet and culture, north into the Slavic world, including Russia. So when you picture Christian Europe, picture two Christendoms: a decentralized Catholic west and a centralized Orthodox Byzantine east, related but distinct.

sections.question: In what way did the Roman Catholic Church play a role in western Europe similar to the role Confucianism played in East Asia or Islam in Dar al-Islam?
options: It governed a centralized bureaucratic empire through civil service exams
It provided a shared cultural and moral framework that unified a politically fragmented region
It rejected all connection to political power and wealth
It was confined to a single kingdom and had no influence beyond it
sections.explanation: Like Confucianism in East Asia and Islam in Dar al-Islam, the Catholic Church supplied a shared identity, scholarly language (Latin), and moral framework that bound together a region with no single political ruler. It did not run a bureaucratic exam-based empire, it was deeply tied to wealth and power, and its influence crossed many kingdoms.

sections.heading: A World Beginning to Change
sections.content:
Europe around 1250 was decentralized and rural, but it was not frozen. Over the next two centuries, forces gathered that would slowly pull it in a new direction — and tracking that change is exactly the kind of continuity-and-change thinking the exam expects.

Contact with the wider world helped. The Crusades (a series of religious wars beginning in 1095, aimed at seizing the Holy Land from Muslim control) failed in their main military goal but had a huge side effect: they reconnected western Europeans with the richer, more sophisticated worlds of the Islamic Mediterranean and Byzantium. Crusaders and the merchants who supplied them brought back goods, knowledge, and a taste for Eastern luxuries, helping revive long-distance trade. Italian cities like Venice and Genoa grew wealthy as middlemen in this commerce.

That trade revival fed a quiet revolution at home: the growth of towns and a money economy. As commerce expanded, towns swelled with merchants and artisans who were not part of the feudal-manorial order. A new urban middle class emerged, and money increasingly mattered more than land and obligation. Meanwhile, some kings began to centralize power at the expense of the nobility, building the foundations of strong monarchies in places like England and France — though not without resistance: in 1215, English nobles forced King John to sign the Magna Carta, limiting royal power and planting an early seed of the idea that even a king is bound by law.

Then came catastrophe. The Black Death, a devastating plague that swept Europe between roughly 1347 and 1351, killed perhaps a third of the population. The human horror was immense — but the social aftershocks accelerated change. With so many workers dead, surviving peasants could suddenly demand wages and freedom, fatally weakening serfdom and the manorial system in much of western Europe. Labor became precious; the old bonds loosened. Out of this turbulent, trade-revived, plague-shaken society, the Renaissance — a flowering of art and learning drawing on rediscovered classical knowledge — was just beginning in the wealthy cities of Italy. Europe in 1450 was still no superpower, but it was a society in motion.

Medieval Europe was decentralized (feudalism and manorialism) and unified mainly by the Catholic Church, but trade revival, growing towns, centralizing monarchies, and the Black Death were already loosening the old order by 1450.

sections.heading: A Worked Comparison: Europe and China Side by Side
sections.content:
Let's model the comparison move the exam demands, using Europe and Song China. The basis of comparison will be: how did each society organize political power, and why?

Start with a genuine similarity. Both were large agrarian societies facing the same fundamental challenge — how to keep order and extract resources from many people spread across a wide territory. Stating this shared problem gives the comparison a spine; without it, you'd just be describing two unrelated places.

Now the meaningful difference. China answered with centralization: a single emperor governing through a professional bureaucracy of scholar-officials selected by examination, funded by a commercialized economy. Europe answered with decentralization: power scattered among hereditary lords bound by feudal oaths, an economy of self-sufficient manors worked by serfs, with the Catholic Church rather than a state providing cultural unity. That is a real, specific contrast — not 'China was different from Europe,' but a precise difference in *how* power was structured.

Finally — and this is what separates a top essay from an average one — explain *why* the difference existed. China had a long unbroken tradition of imperial unity and the wealth to fund a salaried bureaucracy; western Europe had fragmented after the western Roman Empire collapsed and lacked a strong central state, so people improvised security through personal feudal bonds. The difference in structure flowed from a difference in circumstance. Notice the shape of the whole move: similarity → specific difference → causal explanation. Memorize that shape. It is the skeleton of every strong comparison answer, whether the regions are China and Europe, Aztec and Inca, or Mali and the Swahili coast.

sections.question: A strong AP comparison essay does more than state that two societies were different. What additional move most distinguishes a high-scoring comparison?
options: Listing as many facts about each society as possible
Explaining WHY the similarities or differences existed, using historical reasoning
Choosing two societies from completely different time periods
Describing one society in detail and barely mentioning the other
sections.explanation: Top comparisons explain the reasons behind similarities and differences rather than just naming them, turning description into analysis. Piling up facts is not analysis, comparing across mismatched time periods invites chronological errors, and neglecting one society forfeits comparison points entirely.

sections.heading: How to Write a Comparison Essay (LEQ)

steps.title: Contextualize: set the stage (1 point)
steps.content: Open with a sentence or two of relevant background that situates both societies in the wider world of c. 1200–1450 — for example, that this was an era of expanding trade networks and varied forms of state-building across Afro-Eurasia and the Americas. Keep it tied to the prompt; avoid generic 'since the dawn of time' filler.

steps.title: Write a defensible comparative thesis (1 point)
steps.content: Make a specific claim that names both a similarity and a difference (or a clear comparative judgment): 'While both Song China and feudal Europe were large agrarian societies seeking to organize power, China relied on a centralized exam-based bureaucracy whereas Europe relied on decentralized feudal bonds and the unifying authority of the Catholic Church.' Avoid vague theses like 'they were similar in some ways and different in others.'

steps.title: Marshal specific evidence for BOTH societies (up to 2 points)
steps.content: Support your argument with precise, in-period facts about each region — scholar-gentry, paper money, and Champa rice for China; fiefs, serfs, manors, and the Pope for Europe. You must provide real evidence for both sides; describing only one society caps your evidence score. Specificity (name it) is what earns these points.

steps.title: Use reasoning to analyze the comparison (up to 2 points)
steps.content: Explain WHY the similarities or differences existed and what they reveal — for instance, that Europe's decentralization stemmed from the post-Roman absence of a central state, while China's centralization rested on an unbroken imperial tradition and a wealthy economy. Sustained comparative analysis, not just paired description, earns the complexity and analysis points.

sections.heading: The Comparison Essay Killers
sections.content: Three mistakes sink comparison answers. First, the 'parallel description' trap: writing a paragraph on Europe, then a paragraph on China, and never actually comparing them — you must connect the two with words like 'whereas,' 'similarly,' and 'unlike.' Second, neglecting one society: spending 90% of the essay on Europe forfeits points that require evidence and analysis for both. Third, out-of-period evidence: a prompt on 1200–1450 cannot be answered with the Industrial Revolution or the Roman Republic; graders ignore evidence outside the time frame, a documented common error. Stay in the period, weave the societies together, and give both their due.

sections.heading: Build a Comparison Thesis from a Template
sections.content: Under time pressure, a reliable thesis template prevents fumbling: 'While [Society A] and [Society B] both [shared feature], they differed in [specific dimension]: A [did X] whereas B [did Y].' Plug in: 'While Song China and feudal Europe both organized large agrarian populations, they differed in how power was structured: China governed through a centralized bureaucracy chosen by examination, whereas Europe distributed power among hereditary feudal lords.' This template guarantees you name a similarity, a difference, and both societies — the core of the thesis point.

sections.heading: Europe Essentials and Comparison Categories
sections.content: Europe: feudalism (lord–vassal, fiefs, military service) + manorialism (self-sufficient estates, serfs bound to land). Catholic Church = unifying authority (Pope, Latin, monasteries); Schism of 1054 split Catholic west from Orthodox/Byzantine east. Change drivers: Crusades (from 1095, revived trade), growth of towns/money economy, centralizing monarchies, Magna Carta (1215), Black Death (1347–1351, killed ~1/3, weakened serfdom). Useful comparison categories for any states: political structure (centralized vs. decentralized), economy, religion/legitimacy, labor systems, and treatment of trade.

sections.heading: Why the 'Backwater' Question Matters for the Whole Course
sections.content:
Here is a puzzle that should stay with you for the rest of AP World: in 1450, western Europe was one of the *less* impressive regions on the planet — poorer than China, less unified than Dar al-Islam, less wealthy per person than the great trade empires of Africa. Yet within a few centuries, European powers would dominate global trade and build empires spanning the world. How did the apparent backwater end up on top? You cannot answer that yet, and you shouldn't try — but you should plant the question now, because the whole arc of Units 3 through 6 is, in part, the story of how that reversal happened.

And some of the seeds are already visible in this lesson. Europe's very fragmentation — all those competing kingdoms and rival merchant cities — bred relentless competition that would later drive innovation, exploration, and the race for trade routes; no single emperor could shut down a new idea or a risky voyage the way a unified empire might. The trade-hungry Italian cities, the money economy, the centralizing monarchies, the loosening of serfdom after the Black Death — these are the early machinery of the changes to come. Meanwhile, the Black Death itself is not only a European story; it traveled along the very Afro-Eurasian trade networks you'll study in Unit 2, a grim reminder that connection carries disease as well as goods. So end Unit 1 holding two ideas at once: comparison reveals how different the world's societies were around 1200–1450, and the differences you've mapped — especially Europe's odd weakness — are precisely what make the next chapters of world history so dramatic.

On content, emphasize Europe's decentralization (feudalism: lord-vassal-fief; manorialism: serfs bound to self-sufficient manors), the unifying role of the Roman Catholic Church and the 1054 Catholic-Orthodox/Byzantine split, and the forces of change (Crusades, trade revival, growth of towns and a money economy, centralizing monarchies, Magna Carta 1215, and the Black Death of 1347–1351 weakening serfdom). On skills, this lesson explicitly teaches the comparison reasoning process and the LEQ rubric (contextualization, defensible comparative thesis, specific evidence for BOTH societies, and reasoning that explains WHY similarities/differences existed). Watch for the parallel-description trap (describing two societies without comparing), neglecting one society, and out-of-period evidence — all documented exam errors.
